e.t: This Hebrew word expresses being “beside” something or someone, and by extension being “without” that person or thing. It functions as a relational word, marking what is present alongside another or what is excluded from consideration. It occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 16 verses, from Genesis through Jeremiah. The surrounding words determine whether the sense emphasizes accompanying, excepting, or existing apart from something else.

This Hebrew word means “proud.” It functions as a description of a person marked by pride rather than humility. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs once, in Psalm 123:4. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense identifies someone as proud. This is a moral and personal description, expressing an attitude of elevated self-regard. Scripture’s use of the word therefore points to the character or disposition of the people being described, not merely to an outward appearance.

This Hebrew word means “cure” and functions as a verb describing the act of making someone well. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Hosea 5:13. The word presents cure as something sought for a serious condition, though the surrounding verse is needed to explain the full situation. Its sense remains focused on curing rather than merely recognizing an illness or seeking assistance.

This Hebrew word means “sake,” expressing the reason, cause, or purpose connected with an action or situation. It commonly indicates that something happens for the sake of a person, matter, or circumstance. The word appears 10 times in the Old Testament, showing a recurring use for identifying why something occurs or is done. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “love.” It functions as a verb, expressing strong affection or devoted regard toward another person or toward God. Its use can describe love within human relationships as well as love directed toward the LORD. The word occurs 211 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that loving is a broad biblical action involving both people and God. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “axe,” naming a tool used for cutting or shaping wood. It functions as a noun, referring to the implement itself rather than an action. The word appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament: twice in Deuteronomy, once in 1 Kings, and once in Isaiah. Its occurrences include Deuteronomy 19:5, Deuteronomy 20:19, 1 Kings 6:7, and Isaiah 10:15. The exact force of the word in any one verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “drive.” It describes causing a person or group to leave a place or causing something to be removed. The word is used 46 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including situations involving people being sent away and nations being removed from land. Its basic sense is an active movement or expulsion carried out by someone. The surrounding passage determines who is driven and what circumstances are involved, but the word itself focuses on the action of driving out or away.

Hadad-rimmon is a Hebrew term whose precise lexical meaning is not established by the available wording; it appears as a distinct named expression in Zechariah 12:11. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in that one verse. The term is connected there with another Hebrew word through a relationship recorded for the verse, but without the verse text, that connection does not justify adding a meaning or describing its role further.

This Hebrew verb means “imagine.” It describes an act of forming something in the mind, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 62:3. Since the word occurs only there and the verse text is not before us here, its precise force in that sentence belongs to the surrounding context. Its basic lexical sense remains the mental act of imagining.

Uphaz is a proper name used as a distinctive designation in the Hebrew Old Testament. Its preserved meaning is “Uphaz,” rather than a general action, quality, or description. The word occurs only twice in this Hebrew corpus, in Jeremiah 10:9 and Daniel 10:5. Since the name itself does not provide an explicit definition, its precise referent in each passage depends on the surrounding verse text rather than on the name alone.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Ziph.” It identifies a place in the Old Testament, including locations associated with Judah and the wilderness where David was pursued. The word occurs 10 times in 9 Old Testament verses, so it functions as a geographic name rather than a description of a quality, action, or belief. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage and the place being discussed.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “cords.” It names cords as tangible objects and is used as something that can be spoken of, given, or treated as an object within a sentence. The word occurs 62 times in the Old Testament, so its basic sense appears across many passages rather than belonging to only one setting. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses these cords.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “hook,” referring to a physical object used in the Old Testament. It occurs eight times across seven Old Testament verses. The word is used for hooks associated with people or creatures being handled, restrained, or moved, so its ordinary sense remains concrete rather than abstract. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object or person connected with it.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “portion,” a distinct share assigned to or received by someone. It can describe a division of land, goods, or an inheritance, and it may also identify what belongs to a person or group. The word occurs 67 times in the Old Testament, appearing in passages about dividing, receiving, or giving portions. Its broad use shows a portion as something recognized as one person’s or group’s share within a larger whole.

This Hebrew word means “urgent.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a matter or situation that requires immediate attention. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel, so its recorded use is limited rather than broad. The two occurrences are found in Daniel 2:15 and Daniel 3:22. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a description of urgency.

This Hebrew word means “lattice,” naming a lattice or latticework structure. It functions as a concrete noun describing a physical architectural feature. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Song of Solomon 2:9. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its basic meaning points to a screened or gridded structure rather than an action, quality, or person.

This Hebrew word describes “terror”—a condition of frightening dread or alarm. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Genesis 35:5. The available rendering is consistent in both English translations, supporting “terror” as the clearest ordinary meaning. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this cache explains the word’s normal sense rather than the specific way the terror functions in that verse.

“Dew” refers to the moisture that settles on the ground or plants, usually during the night. This Hebrew noun identifies a natural form of surface moisture rather than an action or personal quality. It occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament data, all in Daniel 4–5, and each recorded rendering is “dew.” Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the visible moisture associated with nighttime settling.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to what is “dry,” functioning as a noun for a dry area or condition rather than describing an action. It is used fourteen times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including accounts where water gives way to dry ground and where dry land is recognized in relation to the sea. Its central idea is the absence of water in a place that may otherwise be covered or surrounded by it.

This word is a name or designation for the LORD. It functions as a proper name rather than as a general description of a person, place, or thing. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 17:15, within the same verse. Scripture presents it as a name given to the LORD, so its central meaning is tied to identifying Him. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific significance of that name in context.

The Hebrew word refers to “howling,” describing a loud, sorrowful outcry. It functions as a term for the sound itself rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs five times, in four verses, showing a focused use for this kind of vocal expression. It appears in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Zechariah, including Isaiah 15:8, Jeremiah 25:36, Zephaniah 1:10, and Zechariah 11:3.

Jarha is a personal name in the Hebrew Old Testament, not a common word describing an object, action, or quality. Its role is to identify an individual rather than express a general concept, command, or emotion. The name appears twice in the Hebrew corpus, in 1 Chronicles 2:34 and 2:35. Thus, its ordinary meaning is the proper name “Jarha”; understanding what occurs in either passage requires the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, but its specific meaning is not established by the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:36, so Scripture provides no repeated usage pattern that would clarify a broader sense. The word should therefore be understood as the name of an individual rather than expanded into an unsupported definition or translation. Its precise significance cannot be stated beyond that without additional lexical or contextual information.

This Hebrew word refers to “healing,” the restoration of health or wholeness after harm. It functions as a word describing recovery rather than naming a person or place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Nahum 3:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the removal or relief of injury and the return to a sound condition.

This Hebrew word means “ashamed.” It is a verb describing the experience or condition of being ashamed, whether referring to a person or to people collectively. In the Old Testament, it occurs 38 times, showing that it commonly expresses shame in varied situations. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains the experience of being ashamed.

This Hebrew word means “night,” referring to the period of darkness rather than daytime. It functions as a noun and is used five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel. Its occurrences span Daniel 2:19, Daniel 5:30, and Daniel 7:2, 7, and 13. The word therefore names a time of day and can provide the setting for an event, vision, or action described in the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “cursing” or “rebuke”—words that express condemnation or a forceful correction. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Deuteronomy 28:20. As a rare term, its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense points to a spoken or expressed act of cursing or rebuking rather than a general description of hardship. These two established meanings help readers recognize its role without treating every English rendering as a separate meaning.

This Hebrew word refers to “circumcision,” the bodily rite named in the Old Testament. It functions as a term identifying that act rather than describing a person, quality, or emotion. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs once, in Exodus 4:26. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text, but the word itself points specifically to circumcision. The same meaning is reflected in both recorded English renderings.

Mesha is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Mesha.” It functions as a proper name identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 2:42, and no broader pattern of usage is available from this single occurrence. The name itself does not, by its lexical role, state that person’s character, family history, or significance; those matters must come from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This Hebrew word means “offerings,” referring to gifts or sacrificial items presented in worship. It occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, in Ezra 7:17 and Daniel 2:46. In both passages, it functions as something given or brought as part of an act of honor or service. The word therefore points to an offering presented rather than to the person making it or the action of presenting it. Its exact significance in either passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “slip.” It is used when someone or something loses firm footing or stability, and it can function as the action described in a sentence. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in 2 Samuel, Job, and Psalms. Its repeated use in poetic passages presents slipping as a movement away from a secure position, whether literally or in an expressed picture of instability.

This word refers to “bells”—objects identified by their sound and use. It functions as a noun naming those objects rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Zechariah 14:20. The word’s basic sense is clear, while the particular significance of the bells in that verse must be understood from its surrounding context in that passage.

This Hebrew noun refers to “fining,” the purification of metal by heat or refining. It names the process by which impurities are removed, rather than the person performing it. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in Proverbs, where its established rendering points to this refining process. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the refining image is used there.

This Hebrew word expresses that someone or something “was,” stating a past condition or situation. It functions as a verb within a sentence and may describe a person, object, or circumstance being in a particular state. It occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and sentence. The approved rendering pattern consistently points to “was” as its central meaning.

This Hebrew word describes making something bright or thoroughly scouring it clean. It can refer to cleaning an object until its surface is bright, or to preparing and polishing equipment so it is ready for use. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, with its usage showing this practical sense of cleansing or brightening rather than describing an inward feeling or abstract idea. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “saith” and marks words being declared or spoken. It functions as a speech marker, frequently identifying a statement as something spoken by God or another speaker. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears 376 times, especially in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where it commonly introduces or identifies prophetic declarations. Its repeated connection with speech shows that it points to the act or authority of declaring words, rather than naming a separate object or event.

This Hebrew word means “roaring,” describing a loud, forceful sound. It functions as a sound-description rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Proverbs: Proverbs 19:12 and Proverbs 20:2. Its repeated rendering as “roaring” supports this central meaning. The precise force of the word in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a pronounced sound that can be heard clearly.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “preferred.” It functions as a descriptive term, identifying something or someone regarded as preferred rather than simply naming an action or event. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 6:3. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise role in that sentence cannot be explained further. Its central sense is the description of what is preferred.

This Hebrew word refers to “governors”—officials who exercise authority within a kingdom or government. It functions as a title for people serving in an organized ruling structure, rather than describing ordinary subjects or private individuals. In its five Old Testament occurrences, all in Daniel, it identifies members of the governing body associated with the Babylonian and Medo-Persian realms. The surrounding passage determines each official’s specific responsibilities, but the central meaning remains a recognized civil authority or administrator.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “opinions”—the thoughts or viewpoints a person may hold. It is used as a noun for inward deliberations or competing perspectives, especially when a person is wavering between alternatives. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, in 1 Kings 18:21 and twice in Job. Its setting in speech connects it with expressing or confronting what people think, rather than with a physical object or action.

This Hebrew word means “scribe,” referring to a person identified by that role or title. It functions as a noun for someone associated with writing or official written work. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in Ezra, where it consistently receives the rendering “scribe.” The word’s precise activity in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense identifies the person by this recognized role.

The Hebrew word refers to the place called “Anaharath.” It functions as a proper place name, identifying a specific location rather than describing a quality, action, or object. Since it occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, its ordinary meaning is limited to this geographical identification. The English Bible renderings preserve it as “Anaharath,” and its single occurrence is in Joshua 19:19.

This Hebrew word refers to “anklets,” a noun naming ornaments or items worn around the ankles. It appears twice in the Old Testament, once in Proverbs and once in Isaiah, showing that its ordinary sense is a physical object rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies anklets. Scripture records its use in Proverbs 7:22 and Isaiah 3:18.

Alamoth is a Hebrew term preserved in English as “Alamoth.” It functions as a designation rather than a normally translated descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:20. Because no short definition or surrounding verse text is available here, its precise role in that passage cannot be stated more specifically without adding information beyond the word-level evidence. The term itself is therefore best understood as the proper designation “Alamoth.”

This Hebrew word means “bind,” expressing the action of securing or joining something to something else. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Job 31:36 and once in Proverbs 6:21. In both recorded uses, it functions as an action word involving something being fastened in relation to another thing. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence and its wider context.

This Hebrew word refers to a gathering—the act or result of bringing things or people together. It functions as a noun, naming something collected or assembled rather than describing the action as a verb. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah and Micah, and is rendered “gathering” where English rendering is available. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains collection or assembly.

This word functions as the name “Ittahkazin,” identifying a specific place rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Joshua 19:13. Because no explicit definition is preserved for it, its ordinary meaning is its role as a proper place-name. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular significance there.

This Hebrew word is a place-name rendered “Parah.” It identifies a location mentioned once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 18:23. Because the available wording preserves the name rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive term, its basic meaning for readers is the name of that place. The surrounding verse and passage would be needed to explain Parah’s specific role in Joshua’s geographical list.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. No specific English gloss or short definition is available, so assigning a more precise synonym would be uncertain. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 65:4. That single occurrence makes the surrounding verse and passage necessary for determining its precise force; the reference alone does not establish an expanded meaning. It should therefore be understood cautiously rather than given an unsupported interpretation.

Zelzah is a Hebrew proper name, functioning as a place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 10:2, and English translations preserve it as “Zelzah.” Since it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to a particular named location. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role there.

This Hebrew verb means to “sanctify.” It describes an action performed upon a person, day, place, object, or offering, marking that subject as belonging to God’s holy purpose. The word appears 173 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Haggai, and is especially common in passages concerning worship, priests, sacred things, and appointed times. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word refers to the Kenites, a named people or family group in the Old Testament. It functions as a designation for people rather than as a general description or action. The word occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through 1 Chronicles, and is especially associated with passages involving Israel’s neighboring or connected peoples. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the name “Kenites.”

This Hebrew word is a personal name rendered “Happuch.” As a name, it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, with both occurrences in Job 42:14. The available biblical reference places the word among the names recorded there, so its ordinary function is to designate that named individual. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, not on treating the name as a general description.

This Hebrew verb means “pursued,” describing the act of going after someone or something, often with determined movement toward them. It can refer to a person or group chasing an enemy, seeking to overtake someone, or continuing after a target. The word appears 144 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic sense is broad enough for both pursuit in conflict and ordinary chasing. Its precise force in any verse depends on who is pursuing, whom or what they pursue, and the surrounding passage.

Ramathite is a noun identifying a person connected with a place or family called Ramah. It functions as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:27, and is rendered Ramathite. Without the surrounding verse text, the word itself establishes the person’s association with Ramah but does not provide further details about that individual.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “captives,” people who have been taken and held under another power. It names the persons involved rather than an action, and in its Old Testament uses it can function as the object of verbs describing captives being given, brought, or spoken about. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Deuteronomy through Jeremiah. Its central idea remains people held captive, while the surrounding passage determines the particular circumstances.

This Hebrew verb means “err” or “erred”: to go wrong or stray from what is right. It can describe a person’s mistaken conduct or a failure to follow the proper way. The word occurs 21 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in legal instruction, wisdom writings, poetry, and prophetic passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains wandering into error rather than acting correctly.

e.t: This word refers to “Shushan,” the name of a city. It functions as a place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, especially in Esther, and also appears in Nehemiah and Daniel. Its role is to identify the location named in the passage; the surrounding verse determines what is happening there. The name is consistently rendered “Shushan,” supporting its use as a proper geographical name.

The word refers to a “lyre,” a musical instrument. It names the instrument rather than an action, quality, or person. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 15:21.
